summary: "Mystic Isles of the South Seas" by Frederick O'Brien is a travelogue written during the early 20th century. Through his eyes, readers are introduced to the captivating life of the islands, the warmth of the local inhabitants, and the adventures he encounters along the sapphire lagoons and silver beaches. At the start of the account, the author embarks on a journey aboard the ship Noa-Noa, leaving behind the tumult of San Francisco. The opening illustrates the atmosphere of anticipation and curiosity as he boards, detailing the unusual fellow passengers, including a sorrowful Chinese philosopher who ultimately takes his own life during the journey. O'Brien reflects on various characters, his thoughts about the blissful nature of Tahitian culture, and the tragic clash with Western ideals. As the ship progresses toward Tahiti, O'Brien’s poetic descriptions and rich imagery set the stage for the exploration of the enchanting landscape and its people, unveiling a mixture of joy and melancholy that accompanies his experience in this paradise.
